title: Modesty, a few months on
hook: Maybe you started hijab, or stopped. Maybe you're growing a beard and your family hates it. Wherever you are, let's talk honestly.

screens.text: Three weeks ago, on Day 38, you learned what modesty asks. Since then, real life happened. {women}Maybe you started hijab, or tried and stopped.{/women}{men}Maybe you're growing a beard and getting looks.{/men} Today is a check-in, with no judgment.

**The ruling hasn't changed. Neither has the mercy.** {women}Hijab is required for Muslim women past puberty [Q 24:31].{/women}{men}Modesty is asked of you first [Q 24:30–31]: lowering your gaze, loose clothing covering at least navel to knee, no showing off.{/men}
bubbles: Journeys aren't straight lines. {women}Scholars describe helping new Muslims toward hijab step by step [Qibla 35720].{/women}{men}Modesty can grow in steps, like everything else.{/men}
A step back isn't the end. It's a place to start again.

screens.title: Things people tell themselves. Tap each one.

cards.front: {women}"I took my hijab off for a while. I'm a hypocrite."{/women}{men}"I keep slipping on lowering my gaze. I'm a hypocrite."{/men}
cards.back: {women}No. You're a Muslim who had a hard stretch. The ruling still stands, and so does the way back. Start again when you can, and talk to a sister you trust.{/women}{men}No. You're a Muslim in a hard fight, and struggling isn't denying. Lower it again and keep going.{/men}

cards.front: "She's not covered, so she can't be serious about Islam."
cards.back: You can't see her story or her heart. That judgment isn't yours to make.

cards.front: "If I'm not perfect at it, I shouldn't try at all."
cards.back: A step is a path forward, not permission to stop. Small and steady still counts.

screens.text: **The beard.** The Prophet ﷺ told men to let their beards grow and trim their mustaches [Bukhari 5892]. Many scholars hold that keeping a beard is required; your imam can explain the details.
bubbles: If work or family pushes back, talk to your imam rather than deciding alone.

screens.situation: Marcus has been growing a beard for a month. His mom hates it and keeps asking him to shave before the family reunion.

options.text: Stay kind and patient with his mom, and talk to his imam about it rather than deciding alone
options.feedback: Yes. Kindness to his mom stays, and the imam can help him with his own situation.

options.text: Tell his mom it's required and refuse to discuss it
options.feedback: Not quite. Hard words with a parent rarely help. Stay gentle, and take the question to his imam.

options.text: Shave in secret, feel like a fake, and stop going to the masjid
options.feedback: Not quite. Hiding from the masjid makes everything harder. Stay connected and talk it through instead.

screens.situation: Ana started wearing hijab a month ago. After some ugly comments at work, she took it off. Now she feels like a fake and is thinking about skipping the masjid so no one sees her.

options.text: Keep going to the masjid, talk to a sister or mentor she trusts, and plan a next step she can actually keep
options.feedback: Yes. Staying connected is how people find their way back. One honest next step beats hiding.

options.text: Stay away from the masjid until she's ready to wear it every day
options.feedback: Not quite. Hiding makes it harder. The masjid is for Muslims on the way, which is everyone.

options.text: Decide hijab isn't really required, so there's nothing to feel bad about
options.feedback: Not quite. That's turning a struggle into a denial. Keep the ruling and be gentle with herself.

screens.text: **No judging, either way.** The Qur'an says not to mock others, since they may be better than you [Q 49:11]. That goes for the sister in jeans and the brother who's clean-shaven.
bubbles: It also goes for people who judge *you*. Their comments aren't the ruling, and they aren't your mentor.
**Haya'** (dignity and modesty) is part of faith [Bukhari 9], and it includes how we treat each other.

screens.prompt: Judging others, or minding your own path? Sort each one.

items.text: Whispering about the sister in jeans after prayer
items.why: Mocking and gossip are out. She may be better than you [Q 49:11].

items.text: Assuming the clean-shaven brother isn't serious about Islam
items.why: You can't see his story or his heart. That judgment isn't yours to make.

items.text: Giving everyone at the masjid the same warm welcome
items.why: Yes. Everyone there is on the way. Haya' includes how we treat each other [Bukhari 9].

items.text: Working on your own one step this month
items.why: Yes. Your own path is the one that's yours to work on.

screens.text: **You don't have to carry this alone.** You can ask for a female mentor or staff member at {{masjid.name}} and talk through hijab privately.
bubbles: {teen}If you're under 18 and your parents are against hijab, don't take it on alone.{/teen}
{teen}Talk to a female mentor at {{masjid.name}} and your imam before it becomes a standoff at home.{/teen}
{teen}They'll help you find a way that keeps your faith and your family.{/teen}

screens.text: The ruling stands, the path can be gradual, and nobody's journey is yours to judge, including your own, too harshly.
Modesty grows the way everything else has: one step, kept, then the next.

check.prompt: A sister took her hijab off for a while after harassment. What's true?

options.text: She's a Muslim who had a hard stretch; the ruling stands and the way back is open
options.feedback: Right. Struggling isn't denying, and a step back isn't the end.

options.text: Hijab must not be required for her anymore
options.feedback: Not quite. The ruling stands [Q 24:31]. What's gentle is the pace and the support.

check.prompt: What does the Qur'an say about mocking other Muslims over their practice?

options.text: Don't mock others; they may be better than you
options.feedback: Right [Q 49:11]. You can't see anyone's whole story.

options.text: It's fine if it motivates them
options.feedback: Not quite. Mocking is forbidden [Q 49:11]. Advice, if any, is private and kind.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Hijab is held to be required for women past puberty by mainstream scholars of all four schools [Q 24:31; Q 33:59]; modesty (gaze, dress, conduct) applies to men first [Q 24:30–31]. Haya' is part of faith [Bukhari 9].
- The approach can be gradual: Shaykh Gibril Haddad describes helping a convert toward hijab step by step while the ruling "stands as prescribed" [Qibla 35720]. A sister not covering yet, or who stopped, is a Muslim working toward it, never told it's optional (Q8).
- Beard: the Prophet ﷺ commanded men to let the beard grow and trim the mustache [Bukhari 5892]. Many scholars hold it's required (the Hanafi school holds shaving it is not allowed); others treat it more lightly. Drafted as "many scholars hold it's required; ask your imam" (NEW flag).
- Don't mock or judge [Q 49:11].
- A girl under 18 whose parents oppose hijab: no pressure, no telling her the ruling doesn't apply, no telling her to defy her parents; route to a female mentor and the imam before any standoff (Q27).
- Field Guide ch. 10 covers hijab and modesty for men and women from a convert's angle.

**Likely questions**
- *"I stopped wearing hijab. Am I a bad Muslim?"* No shame. She's a Muslim who had a hard stretch. Ask what made it hard (safety, work, family, feeling alone); suggest small steps and a female mentor.
- *"My family hates my beard / my hijab."* Acknowledge it. Kindness to parents [Q 31:14–15]. Don't rule; route to the imam, and for women, a female mentor if wanted.
- *"Is the beard really required?"* Give the hadith and "many scholars hold it's required"; offer "Ask my imam". Don't shame clean-shaven men.
- *"Brothers have it easy."* (a sister's frustration) Men's modesty is real too: lowering the gaze, loose clothing covering at least navel to knee, no showing off. It's just less visible. Don't turn it into a comparison; keep the focus on her own path.
- *"People at the masjid judge me."* Validate; their comments aren't rulings. Suggest a trusted sister/brother or the mentor; Day 48 for when Muslims let you down.
- *"I'm being harassed for wearing hijab."* Safety first; Day 52 (CAIR). Workplace accommodation: Day 38.

**Escalate:** a minor whose parents oppose hijab (Q27: female mentor and imam); safety threats linked to visible dress (safety rule; CAIR); a job requiring removal of hijab or shaving (imam; CAIR for rights); any question about the extent of 'awrah in her own case (female mentor or imam).

**Don't**
- Don't call hijab optional, or say a step back cancels someone's Islam.
- Don't pressure anyone with a timeline, or with Hell.
- Don't comment on anyone's appearance.
- Don't tell a teen to defy her parents, or that the ruling doesn't apply to her.
